newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan slams Japan's naval snub at disputed isles.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan slams Japan's naval snub at disputed isles.

text.p: Taiwan's foreign ministry on Friday angrily protested Japan's use of coast guard vessels to force a private Taiwanese ship away from a chain of East China Sea islands claimed by Taipei, Tokyo and Beijing.
"The Ministry of Foreign Affairs expresses its serious regret over the Japanese government's action," the ministry said in the latest twist of a simmering sovereignty row.

"It hereby reiterates the Diaoyu islands are part of our existing territory. This position is unquestionable," the statement said. "The (Taiwan) government's determination to protect our territory will never change."
The China Times Express said on Thursday that two Japanese patrol boats and a Japanese helicopter turned away a private fishing boat the newspaper had leased for an inspection tour.
The newspaper hoped to check whether Japan had removed a makeshift lighthouse erected by a Japanese right-wing group in July on one island, rekindling the perennial dispute.
The paper said one of the Japanese coast guard ships carried a banner in Chinese reading, "The Japanese government asks you to leave Japan's territorial waters at once."
The small Diaoyu chain lies about 300 km (190 miles) west of Okinawa and 200 km (125 miles) east of Taiwan.

Taiwan television said a second private fishing boat that left for the islands before dawn on Friday was also escorted away by Japanese patrol boats -- but not before burning a Japanese flag aboard their vessel.
"They told us these were Japanese territorial waters and asked us to leave immediately," Taipei county councillor Chin Chieh-shou, who organised the trip, told the television.
"They also said our move was illegal," he added.
Taiwan's foreign ministry said it was "delighted" by the show of patriotism and urged Japan to restrain itself.
"Japan must exercise self-control and not create further incidents in waters near the Diaoyu islands...to avoid damaging our friendship and development of bilateral relations," it said.
Taiwan has no diplomatic ties with Japan, which recognises only Beijing's communist government.
Japan's moves to assert sovereignty over the Diaoyus have angered Chinese in Taiwan, Hong Kong and the Chinese mainland.
In Hong Kong, pro-democracy legislator Tsang Kin-shing vowed to sail to Diaoyus with fellow democrats in October.
Taiwan's parliament was furious. "We should be prepared to fight," one lawmaker told the body on Friday.

Patriotic passion soared in Taiwan in July after discovery of the lighthouse built by the rightist Japan Youth Federation, with 200 Taiwan fishing boats threatening to storm the island to dismantle the structure.
The protest was cancelled in August after Tokyo officials came to Taiwan to discuss the simmering row. The Japanese group halted plans to further assert Tokyo's claim to the islands.
Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government and Beijing's communist People's Republic that toppled it both assert that China has had sovereignty over the islands for centuries.
Tokyo's claim dates to Japan's military humiliation of China in 1895, when it wrested Taiwan and other Chinese territories as war booty to be used as a base for wider Asian conquests.
